title: Introduction to Accounting
description: Class 11 Accountancy: meaning, objectives and functions of accounting, internal and external users, branches of accounting, advantages and limitations, and the basic accounting terms you must know.

topics.title: Meaning, Objectives and Functions of Accounting
topics.concept:
Accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, recording and communicating the financial information of a business to its users. In one sentence: accounting is the language of business — it tells the owner and others how much the business earned, spent, owns and owes.

It helps to separate three terms students often confuse:

  • Book-keeping — only the recording part: writing transactions in the books day to day. It is routine and clerical.
  • Accounting — a wider process that summarises, analyses and interprets what book-keeping has recorded, and reports it.
  • Accountancy — the whole body of knowledge (the rules, principles and practice) that governs accounting.

So the order is: Accountancy → Accounting → Book-keeping, from the widest to the narrowest.

The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) defined accounting as "the art of recording, classifying and summarising in a significant manner and in terms of money, transactions and events which are, in part at least, of a financial character, and interpreting the results thereof."

The objectives of accounting are to: (i) keep a systematic record of transactions; (ii) ascertain the profit or loss of the business; (iii) ascertain the financial position (assets and liabilities) through the balance sheet; (iv) provide information to users for decisions; and (v) help in compliance with legal requirements such as tax.

The main functions follow from the definition — recording, classifying, summarising, dealing only with what can be measured in money, and analysing & interpreting the results so that decisions can be made.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why is accounting called the "language of business"?
examples.solution:
It communicates financial facts.

  • Just as language conveys ideas, accounting conveys the financial results and position of a business.
  • It lets owners, lenders and others understand how the business is doing.
examples.answer: Because, like a language, it communicates the financial results and position of a business to all who need that information.

examples.solution:
Recording vs interpreting.

  • Book-keeping is only the routine recording of transactions.
  • Accounting is wider — it also summarises, analyses and interprets, then reports the information.
examples.answer: Book-keeping is just the recording of transactions; accounting is wider, also summarising, analysing, interpreting and communicating the results.

examples.problem: Example 3: State any two objectives of accounting.
examples.solution:
Pick from the standard list.

  • To keep a systematic record of transactions.
  • To ascertain the profit or loss and the financial position of the business.
examples.answer: To keep a systematic record of transactions, and to ascertain the profit or loss and financial position of the business.

recap:
• Accounting = identifying, measuring, recording & communicating financial information — the language of business.
  • Width: Accountancy → Accounting → Book-keeping (widest to narrowest). Book-keeping = recording only.
  • Objectives: systematic records, profit/loss, financial position, information to users, legal compliance.

quiz.explanation: Accounting communicates financial information, so it is the language of business.

quiz.q: Which is the narrowest of these terms?
quiz.explanation: Book-keeping (just recording) is the narrowest; accountancy is the widest.

topics.title: Users of Accounting Information and Branches of Accounting
topics.concept:
Accounting is useful only because people use the information it produces. These users fall into two groups.

Internal users (inside the business)External users (outside the business)
Owners / proprietors — to know profit and returnInvestors & potential investors — safety and return
Management — to plan and controlLenders & banks — can the business repay?
Employees & their unions — pay, bonus, job securityCreditors / suppliers — will they be paid on time?
 Government & tax authorities — taxes, regulation
 Customers and researchers / public — continuity, data

Because different users need different information, accounting has grown into specialised branches:

  • Financial accounting — records transactions and prepares the profit & loss account and balance sheet for outside users. (This is the focus of Class 11.)
  • Cost accounting — ascertains the cost of products and services and helps control costs.
  • Management accounting — presents accounting information to management for planning, decision-making and control.

The two main qualities that make accounting information useful for all these users are reliability (free from error and bias, verifiable) and relevance (it must help the decision at hand). Information should also be understandable and comparable across years and firms.

examples.problem: Example 1: Classify the following as internal or external users: (a) the proprietor, (b) a bank giving a loan, (c) the tax department, (d) the management.
examples.solution:
Inside vs outside the business.

  • Internal: the proprietor and the management.
  • External: the bank and the tax department.
examples.answer: Internal: proprietor and management. External: bank (lender) and tax department.

examples.problem: Example 2: Which branch of accounting helps management make decisions?
examples.solution:
By name.

  • Management accounting presents information to management for planning, decisions and control.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why is a supplier (creditor) interested in a firm's accounts?
examples.solution:
Credit risk.

  • A supplier who sells on credit wants to know whether the firm can pay on time.
  • The accounts show the firm's liquidity and ability to pay.
examples.answer: To judge whether the firm is financially sound enough to pay for goods supplied on credit.

recap:
• Internal users: owners, management, employees. External users: investors, lenders/banks, creditors, government, customers, public.
  • Branches: financial accounting (statements for outsiders), cost accounting (cost of products), management accounting (info for management).
  • Useful information is reliable, relevant, understandable and comparable.

quiz.q: Which of these is an external user of accounting information?
quiz.explanation: A bank is outside the business — an external user. Management, owner and employees are internal.

quiz.q: The branch that ascertains the cost of products is:
quiz.explanation: Cost accounting determines and controls the cost of products and services.

topics.title: Advantages, Limitations and Basic Accounting Terms
topics.concept:
Like any tool, accounting has clear advantages but also real limitations — a good student must know both.

Advantages: it replaces memory with a permanent record; it helps ascertain profit and financial position; it provides evidence in legal matters; it helps in comparing performance over years; it assists in valuing the business when sold; and it helps in assessing tax and raising loans.

Limitations:

  • It records only what can be measured in money, so it ignores valuable things like the skill of staff or customer goodwill that cannot be priced.
  • It is affected by the personal judgement of the accountant (e.g. choice of depreciation method), so figures are estimates, not exact truths.
  • It may ignore the effect of changing price levels (assets are shown at historical cost, not current value).
  • It can be window-dressed — manipulated to look better than reality.

Finally, every accountancy student must master the basic terms — the vocabulary used throughout the course:

TermMeaning
CapitalAmount the owner invests in the business (owner's claim).
DrawingsCash or goods the owner withdraws for personal use.
AssetsResources owned by the business (cash, building, stock, debtors).
LiabilitiesAmounts the business owes to others (creditors, loans).
DebtorA person who owes money to the business (we sold on credit).
CreditorA person to whom the business owes money (we bought on credit).
Revenue / IncomeAmount earned, e.g. from sales or services.
ExpenseCost incurred to earn revenue (rent, salary, wages).
PurchasesGoods bought for resale.
Goods / Stock (Inventory)Items the business deals in; unsold stock is inventory.

Knowing these terms precisely is the foundation for everything that follows — the accounting equation, journal, ledger and final accounts all use them.

examples.problem: Example 1: Give one limitation of accounting linked to money measurement.
examples.solution:
Only money items are recorded.

  • Accounting records only transactions measurable in money.
  • So valuable non-money facts (staff skill, customer loyalty) are ignored.
examples.answer: It records only money-measurable items, so it ignores valuable non-monetary facts such as staff skill and customer goodwill.

examples.problem: Example 2: A owes Rs 5,000 to our business for goods sold on credit. Is A a debtor or a creditor?
examples.solution:
They owe us.

  • A owes money to the business → A is a debtor.
examples.answer: A is a debtor (a person who owes money to the business).

examples.problem: Example 3: The owner takes Rs 2,000 cash from the business for personal use. What is this called?
examples.solution:
Owner withdrawing.

  • Cash or goods taken by the owner for personal use are called drawings.

recap:
• Advantages: permanent record, profit & position, legal evidence, comparison, valuation, tax/loans.
  • Limitations: only money items, personal judgement (estimates), ignores price-level change, can be window-dressed.
  • Key terms: capital, drawings, assets, liabilities, debtor (owes us), creditor (we owe), revenue, expense, purchases, stock.

quiz.q: Cash or goods withdrawn by the owner for personal use are called:
quiz.explanation: Withdrawals by the owner for personal use are drawings.

quiz.q: A person to whom the business owes money is a:
quiz.explanation: We owe a creditor; a debtor owes us.

questions.q: Accounting is best described as the:
questions.explanation: Accounting communicates financial information — the language of business.

questions.q: The routine recording of day-to-day transactions is called:
questions.explanation: Book-keeping is only the recording part of accounting.

questions.q: Arrange from widest to narrowest:
questions.explanation: Accountancy is the body of knowledge, accounting the process, book-keeping the recording.

questions.q: Which is NOT an objective of accounting?
questions.explanation: Accounting serves financial information needs, not personal fame.

questions.q: Which of these is an internal user of accounting information?
questions.explanation: Management is inside the business — an internal user.

questions.q: Investors and lenders are ____ users.
questions.explanation: They are outside the business, so external users.

questions.q: The branch that prepares the profit & loss account and balance sheet for outsiders is:
questions.explanation: Financial accounting prepares the statements used by external users.

questions.q: Amount invested by the owner in the business is called:
questions.explanation: The owner's investment is capital.

questions.q: Goods bought for resale are recorded as:
questions.explanation: Goods bought for resale are purchases.

questions.q: A person who owes money to the business is a:
questions.explanation: A debtor owes money to the business.

questions.q: A person to whom the business owes money is a:
questions.explanation: We owe a creditor.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of accounting?
questions.explanation: Ignoring non-monetary facts is a real limitation.

questions.q: Two qualities that make accounting information useful are:
questions.explanation: Information should be reliable and relevant (also understandable, comparable).

questions.q: Cash withdrawn by the owner for personal use is:
questions.explanation: Owner's withdrawals are drawings.

questions.q: Manipulating accounts to look better than reality is called:
questions.explanation: Presenting a misleadingly favourable picture is window dressing.

questions.q: A firm employs a brilliant, highly motivated team, yet its books show nothing about this. Which limitation explains it?
questions.explanation: Staff quality cannot be measured in money, so the money-measurement limitation excludes it from the books.

questions.q: A shopkeeper says, 'I never write anything down; I remember everything.' The strongest accounting argument against this is that records:
options: Provide a permanent, reliable evidence that memory cannot
questions.explanation: A key advantage of accounting is replacing fallible memory with permanent, verifiable records.

questions.q: Ramesh sold goods to Suresh on credit. In Ramesh's books, Suresh is a ____; in Suresh's books, Ramesh is a ____.
questions.explanation: Suresh owes Ramesh (debtor to Ramesh); Ramesh is owed by Suresh, so Ramesh is Suresh's creditor.

questions.q: A bank deciding whether to lend to a firm is mainly interested in the firm's:
questions.explanation: As an external lender, the bank uses the accounts to judge repayment capacity.

questions.q: Choosing a depreciation method changes the reported profit. This illustrates which limitation?
options: It is the language of business
questions.explanation: Accounting figures depend on the accountant's judgement, so they are estimates rather than exact truths.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly shows the accounting process?
questions.explanation: Transactions are identified, recorded, classified, summarised and finally communicated to users.

questions.q: A manager wants a report comparing the cost of two products to decide which to expand. The most relevant branch is:
questions.explanation: Determining and comparing product costs is the work of cost accounting.

questions.q: Why are 'drawings' never treated the same as a business expense?
options: They are the owner's personal use, not a cost of earning revenue
They are a liability of outsiders
questions.explanation: Drawings reduce the owner's capital; they are personal, not incurred to earn business revenue.

questions.q: Two firms use different methods, making their profits hard to compare. Which quality of useful information is weakened?
questions.explanation: Comparability requires consistent methods so figures can be meaningfully compared across firms and years.

questions.q: A company presents its accounts to hide weak performance before a loan application. This is:
questions.explanation: Dressing up accounts to mislead users is window dressing — a limitation/abuse of accounting.
